transcript:
Header:
Date: 2025-10-21
Start time: 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~42 minutes
Attendees: Alex Kim (Redwood AE), Priya Shah (Redwood SE), Jordan Lee (Redwood Solutions), Martin Lopez (FinEdge, CTO), Sara Chen (FinEdge, ML Eng), Liam O'Neill (FinEdge, PM)

Summary:
Quick hosted API walkthrough focused on chat/text generation basics: streaming responses, common generation parameters (temperature, top_p, max_tokens), handling retries and idempotency, SDK examples, and brief Console/Optimize overview. Customer interested in latency/cost tradeoffs and safe retry semantics for their transactional workflows.

00:00 - Speaker 1 (Alex): hey everyone thanks for joining, yeah uh quick intros from our side, alex kim i'm the ae, priya is our se, jordan will help with the billing and infra questions later
00:12 - Speaker 2 (Martin): hi all, martin here, thanks for running this, we're trying to evaluate hosted API for chat features in FinEdge app, a few questions on latency and retries up front
00:25 - Speaker 3 (Priya): cool, we'll cover streaming and retry patterns and show the console too, want to start with a 5-min overview of the API then demo live calls
00:40 - Speaker 1 (Alex): perfect, outline: api basics, parameters, streaming, retry/backoff, console demo, optimize recommendations, q&a and next steps
01:05 - Speaker 3 (Priya): so the hosted api supports chat & text generation, streaming via chunked responses (SSE-like), and we have SDKs that handle streaming events, chunk parsing, and reconnects for you
01:22 - Speaker 4 (Sara): does streaming use websockets or server-sent events?
01:28 - Speaker 3 (Priya): both patterns are supported by our SDKs; underlying api offers chunked http streaming (sse style) and websocket wrapper in the sdk. generally chunked http is simplest for server-to-server streaming
02:00 - Speaker 3 (Priya): quick demo, curl to show param set: temperature, top_p, max_tokens, stop tokens, and also role/assistant messages for chat. i'll paste a curl now
02:15 - Speaker 3 (Priya): curl -X POST https://api.redwood.ai/v1/chat -H "Authorization: Bearer <KEY>" -d '{"messages":[{"role":"user","content":"Summarize today's market news"}], "temperature":0.2, "max_tokens":300}'
02:40 - Speaker 2 (Martin): nice, and default limits? like token limits and rate limits?
02:48 - Speaker 3 (Priya): default model limits depend on model, but hosted API defaults we expose in the console — typically 8k to 32k context for common models, rate limits per account are configurable, and we provide clear headers for X-RateLimit-Remaining etc
03:20 - Speaker 1 (Alex): martin, for your transactional flows you mentioned low latency was important, can you remind us qps and critical latency percentile goals?
03:30 - Speaker 4 (Martin): we target 95th perc < 300ms for short prompts (~200 tokens) and around 100-200 rps for peak traffic, though pilot will start smaller
03:45 - Speaker 3 (Priya): ok noted, for that profile we suggest a low-latency model variant and enabled prefix caching if you have repeated system prompts, plus aggressive batching on the dedicated side but for hosted we do adaptive batching to preserve latency SLOs
04:12 - Speaker 3 (Priya): now streaming — live demo with node sdk. i'll run a chat stream and show partial tokens as they arrive. watch the console logs, you'll see chunk events and a final done event
04:30 - Speaker 3 (Priya): [typing / demo noise] ok starting stream... client.on('data', chunk => { console.log(chunk.text) }) // pseudo code
05:00 - Speaker 5 (Liam): in the stream if connection drops what's the recommended recovery? can we resume?
05:12 - Speaker 3 (Priya): good q — we support resumable streams only for certain workloads; more common pattern is idempotent requests with a request_id header. if you re-issue with same request_id, server will either return cached result or reject duplicate processing. for long streaming generation, we recommend using checkpointed outputs and re-requesting missing chunks from the start if needed
05:45 - Speaker 3 (Priya): also, our SDK does an automatic reconnect with backoff and can re-request if a final token wasn't received. we also provide a retry guide — e.g., exponential backoff, jitter, and safe status codes (429, 503) vs client errors (4xx)
06:12 - Speaker 2 (Martin): so we should use idempotency keys for safety?
06:20 - Speaker 3 (Priya): yep, include X-Idempotency-Key for create-like calls. for chat you can include a deterministic id so retries are safe. also include a checksum/ prompt fingerprint so you can detect divergent completions
06:50 - Speaker 1 (Alex): let's flip to generation params — quick primer: temperature lower (0-0.3) is deterministic, 0.7 more creative, top_p is nucleus sampling, max_tokens limits length, presence/ frequency penalties for repetition control, and stop sequences to truncate responses early
07:22 - Speaker 4 (Sara): any guidance for transactional replies — e.g., confirmation messages — should we use greedy output?
07:30 - Speaker 3 (Priya): for deterministic transactional messages set temperature 0-0.2 and top_p 0.1-0.5, and validate output server-side. also use safety checks and post-processing rules in case of hallucination. logging and eval hooks can help catch regressions
08:00 - Speaker 3 (Priya): demo: updating params in console — i'll change temperature from 0.2 to 0.0 and show latency & token cost difference in the console trace. you can see token-level cost and latency per-chunk in the console traces
08:25 - Speaker 5 (Liam): is there a way to preset param templates for different routes?
08:30 - Speaker 3 (Priya): yes we have per-route profiles, you can pin configs to a route or model and roll them out. this helps standardize behavior across environments
09:00 - Speaker 3 (Priya): now retries in more detail: exponential backoff starting at 200ms, doubling with jitter, cap at ~10s and 3-5 retries for transient 5xx/429. don't retry on 4xx except for specific cases like 409 with idempotency semantics
09:30 - Speaker 2 (Martin): what about partial charges for aborted streams? billing nuance?
09:38 - Speaker 1 (Alex): good point — we bill per token emitted + prefix tokens; aborted streams where tokens were emitted are billed; we also provide cost previews in the console for sample prompts so you can simulate cost before heavy testing
10:00 - Speaker 3 (Priya): show streaming resilience: SDK handles incremental parsing; if connection fails we surface a retriable error with reason fields. also headers include request-id for follow-up support and we log full trace in console if you have advanced logging enabled
10:45 - Speaker 4 (Martin): security/compliance — we need SOC2, SSO/SAML, customer-managed keys (KMS), and data retention options. do you support those in hosted?
11:00 - Speaker 1 (Alex): yes hosted has enterprise options: SOC 2, SAML SSO, RBAC, per-tenant data retention settings, and optional bring-your-own-key via cloud KMS integrations. for stricter needs we recommend private deployment but hosted enterprise can be configured to meet many requirements
11:35 - Speaker 3 (Priya): also audit logs and request-level metadata are available via the console and can be exported to logging sinks for compliance audits
12:10 - Speaker 3 (Priya): back to demos — showing sample retry code in python. pseudo: 
12:25 - Speaker 3 (Priya): try: resp = client.chat.create(..., idempotency_key=req_id) except TransientError: backoff and retry 
12:45 - Speaker 5 (Liam): do you enforce strict schema on JSON outputs? we have downstream parsers that rely on structured output
12:52 - Speaker 3 (Priya): yes we support structured output and function/tool calling. you can request json schema enforcement, and we have a 'structured' mode that returns JSON or signals parsing errors. we also have a tool-calling pattern where model responses map to tool invocations
13:20 - Speaker 4 (Sara): curious about latency numbers for streaming vs non-streaming — what delta should we expect?
13:30 - Speaker 3 (Priya): streaming often reduces apparent latency because tokens are delivered as generated; total tail latency similar but first-byte can be 50-200ms faster depending on model and prompt. non-streaming requires full generation before the client sees anything
14:00 - Speaker 3 (Priya): show console trace of a streaming vs non-streaming request — observe chunk timings and token counts, cost per token. console also breaks down latency by kernel/compute and network phases (approx)
14:35 - Speaker 3 (Priya): discuss Optimize quick tips: for cost, consider quantized model variants, prefix caching, and token limits. Optimize will suggest model/quantization combos based on workload and supply batching recommendations
15:05 - Speaker 2 (Martin): will Optimize auto-apply suggestions or is it advisory?
15:12 - Speaker 3 (Priya): advisory by default, you can enable automated rollouts for non-prod routes. for production we recommend reviewing suggestions and doing an A/B or canary first
15:40 - Speaker 1 (Alex): question from jordan re: how to debug production errors quickly?
15:50 - Speaker 6 (Jordan): yeah if a customer sees 5xx spikes how do they trace root cause?
15:56 - Speaker 3 (Priya): console has per-request traces and we preserve sample full transcripts with request-id. you can also sample token-level traces and see which kernel or quantization path was used. for infra-level issues we surface capacity alarms and fallback events in the console
16:30 - Speaker 4 (Martin): for pilot we likely want hosted sandbox keys + a small burst plan, plus ability to lift to dedicated if performance needs grow. what's the timeline to scale?
16:42 - Speaker 1 (Alex): typically pilots take 2-4 weeks; if you need Dedicated we can provision reserved capacity in 2-6 weeks depending on region and GPUs. private deployments longer (~8-12 weeks) due to network/setup
17:10 - Speaker 3 (Priya): note on retries again — for idempotent designs, prefer idempotency-key and 409 handling, and consider de-duplicating on your side. also instrument latency percentiles and token counts to detect anomalies
17:40 - Speaker 5 (Liam): any gotchas with streaming and mobile clients?
17:46 - Speaker 3 (Priya): mobile clients can use a gateway pattern: keep short-lived websocket to a server, server streams to client. avoid long-lived mobile streams if network flaky; server-side aggregator improves reliability and reduces mobile battery/network usage
18:10 - Speaker 3 (Priya): quick off-the-cuff cost example: a 200-token prompt + 300-token completion at $0.0008 per token equivalent (example) — costs vary by model; console will show exact cost per model/route
18:35 - Speaker 4 (Sara): are there rate-limiting headers and webhook for quota alerts?
18:40 - Speaker 3 (Priya): yes x-rate-limit-* headers and optional webhook/alerting integrations; console can create usage alerts for thresholds
19:00 - Speaker 1 (Alex): moving to Q&A — martin any open technical blockers?
19:08 - Speaker 4 (Martin): mainly security + predictable latency. also we need SAML + KMS support in hosted or else must go private which is fine but prefer to see hosted enterprise option first
19:25 - Speaker 3 (Priya): we'll attach SOC2 and KMS integration docs in the follow-up, and show sample SAML setup flow for testing in a sandbox tenant
19:45 - Speaker 5 (Liam): for evals, can you share example prompt sets and eval harnesses?
19:50 - Speaker 3 (Priya): yes we have evaluation harness templates and can share sample prompt collections; Optimize can run regression monitoring against them
20:10 - Speaker 2 (Martin): for the pilot, what telemetry do you need from us?
20:18 - Speaker 3 (Priya): basic telemetry: qps, average prompt size, typical completion length, success criteria (latency percentiles), and any safety/regulatory checks you need us to run. we'll provide instrumentation guidance
20:40 - Speaker 1 (Alex): recap next steps live: alex will send pricing & enterprise pack, priya will share streaming sdk and retry docs, martin will send workloads and qps estimates, schedule pilot kickoff 2025-10-27
21:00 - Speaker 3 (Priya): final note: sample sdk snippet for reconnect/backoff: on error if status in [429,502,503] then exponential backoff w/ jitter and re-request with same idempotency key. avoid blind retries on 400s. also log request-id for support
21:35 - Speaker 4 (Martin): thanks, this was helpful. one last quick question: do you provide any SLA for hosted?
21:42 - Speaker 1 (Alex): hosted has SLA options on enterprise plans and dedicated has stronger SLA commitments; we'll include SLA language in the enterprise packet we send
22:00 - Speaker 6 (Jordan): small nit — earlier you said KV cash — do you mean KV cache?
22:05 - Speaker 3 (Priya): yes sorry, KV cache, autocorrect in the notes sometimes messes up our transcripts
22:20 - Speaker 1 (Alex): ok we'll wrap. thanks everyone, follow-ups in email.
